title: The Mathematics Under Cryptography
description: Explore the number theory, probability and hardness assumptions behind selected cryptographic constructions, from clock arithmetic to lattices and pairings.

stops.label: Modular Arithmetic
stops.note: Start with the clock: Z/nZ, primitive roots, and the cyclic group Diffie–Hellman lives inside (§143).

stops.label: Group Theory
stops.note: Generators, order, cyclic structure — the grammar of the discrete-log family (§149).

stops.label: Finite Fields
stops.note: Arithmetic in a finite field and elliptic-curve addition; secure discrete-log parameters require more than a small scatter plot (§142).

stops.label: The Prime Number Theorem
stops.note: Prime density helps estimate how many random candidates a key generator must test (§144).

stops.label: Euler & Fermat
stops.note: The theorem that makes RSA decryption undo encryption. Watch a message round-trip (§145).

stops.label: Elliptic Curves over R
stops.note: The group law drawn by hand — a gentle first look before the curve moves to a finite field (§150).

stops.label: The Ground Beneath the Curve
stops.note: Explore the modularity theorem as mathematical context, separate from the assumptions used to secure ECC (§141).

stops.label: The One-Way Function
stops.note: Efficient forward computation and conjectured inversion hardness; a small factorization example illustrates the distinction (§146).

stops.label: Reduction & Proof
stops.note: A reduction transfers an efficient solution between problems; its direction and assumptions matter (§148).

stops.label: Information & Entropy
stops.note: Shannon entropy measures uncertainty in a distribution. Key length alone does not establish unpredictability (§151).

stops.label: The Random Oracle
stops.note: An ideal random function used in some security proofs. An avalanche display does not validate that idealization (§154).

stops.label: Lattices & the SVP
stops.note: Explore a two-dimensional lattice; practical lattice cryptography uses high dimensions and specific assumptions (§147).

stops.label: The Closest Vector Problem
stops.note: Compare approximate rounding with the nearest point in a small lattice; basis shape affects the heuristic (§152).

stops.label: Learning With Errors
stops.note: t = As + e: solve for the secret, then switch the noise on and watch exact algebra fail (§157).

stops.label: Polynomial Rings
stops.note: R_q = Z_q[X]/(X^n+1): the structured lattice inside ML-KEM and ML-DSA (§153).

stops.label: Polynomial Interpolation
stops.note: Distinct field coordinates determine a polynomial of bounded degree, the arithmetic behind Shamir sharing (§155).

stops.label: Bilinear Pairings
stops.note: Bilinearity supports constructions such as BLS signatures and some proof systems. This is a scalar model, not a cryptographic pairing implementation (§156).
